segments.text: The gambler's fallacy.
segments.caption: The gambler's fallacy.

segments.text: A true story from a casino, the simple maths, a million-flip test, and how it fools you every day. Save this one!
segments.caption: A true story from a casino, the simple maths, a million-flip test, and how it fools you every day. Save this one!

segments.text: You flip a fair coin five times. Heads, heads, heads, heads, heads.
segments.caption: You flip a fair coin five times. Heads, heads, heads, heads, heads.

segments.text: What's the next flip more likely to be? Heads, tails, or fifty-fifty? Comment your answer before I tell you.
segments.caption: What's the next flip more likely to be? Heads, tails, or 50-50? Comment your answer before I tell you.

segments.text: Monte Carlo, 1913. At the roulette table, the ball lands on black. Again. And again.
segments.caption: Monte Carlo, 1913. At the roulette table, the ball lands on black. Again. And again.

segments.text: After ten blacks, the crowd is sure red is due. They bet more and more on red.
segments.caption: After 10 blacks, the crowd is sure red is due. They bet more and more on red.

segments.text: Black came up twenty-six times in a row. The gamblers lost millions. The casino won.
segments.caption: Black came up 26 times in a row. The gamblers lost millions. The casino won.

segments.text: So, the coin. The answer is fifty-fifty. Still.
segments.caption: So, the coin. The answer is 50-50. Still.

segments.text: A coin has no memory. It doesn't know what happened before. Each flip is a brand new event.
segments.caption: A coin has no memory. It doesn't know what happened before. Each flip is a brand new event.

segments.text: Statisticians call this independence: the past flips don't change the next one.
segments.caption: Statisticians call this independence: the past flips don't change the next one.

segments.text: So why does tails feel due? Because five heads in a row feels rare. And it is: one in thirty-two.
segments.caption: So why does tails feel due? Because five heads in a row feels rare. And it is: 1 in 32.

segments.text: But that was before you started. Once those five heads have happened, they're history. The only question left is one flip: half, half.
segments.caption: But that was before you started. Once those five heads have happened, they're history. The only question left is one flip: half, half.

segments.text: Your brain expects small samples to look balanced. The law of large numbers only works over thousands of flips, not five.
segments.caption: Your brain expects small samples to look balanced. The law of large numbers only works over thousands of flips, not five.

segments.text: Don't trust me? We flipped a coin one million times on a computer.
segments.caption: Don't trust me? We flipped a coin one million times on a computer.

segments.text: Five heads in a row happened thirty-one thousand times. And the very next flip? Heads exactly fifty percent of the time.
segments.caption: 5 heads in a row happened 31,000 times. And the very next flip? Heads exactly 50% of the time.

segments.text: And Monte Carlo? Twenty-six in a row is about one in sixty-six million. Incredibly rare.
segments.caption: And Monte Carlo? 26 in a row is about 1 in 66 million. Incredibly rare.

segments.text: But even after twenty-five blacks, the next spin was still the same 48.6 percent for black. Rare streaks happen. They just don't change the odds.
segments.caption: But even after 25 blacks, the next spin was still the same 48.6% for black. Rare streaks happen. They just don't change the odds.

segments.text: It fools us everywhere.
segments.caption: It fools us everywhere.

segments.text: A couple with three boys thinks the fourth must be a girl. It's still about fifty-fifty.
segments.caption: A couple with three boys thinks the fourth must be a girl. It's still about 50-50.

segments.text: A captain who lost five tosses thinks he's due to win the next one. The coin doesn't care.
segments.caption: A captain who lost five tosses thinks he's due to win the next one. The coin doesn't care.

segments.text: And people avoid last week's lottery numbers. They're exactly as likely as any others.
segments.caption: And people avoid last week's lottery numbers. They're exactly as likely as any others.

segments.text: And watch out for the opposite mistake too: thinking heads is hot, so heads will continue. That's also wrong for a fair coin.
segments.caption: And watch out for the opposite mistake too: thinking heads is hot, so heads will continue. That's also wrong for a fair coin.

segments.text: But careful: this only applies to truly random, independent events. A batter in form, or a slot machine that's rigged? Different story.
segments.caption: But careful: this only applies to truly random, independent events. A batter in form, or a slot machine that's rigged? Different story.

segments.text: So remember: random events have no memory. The past doesn't make anything due.
segments.caption: So remember: random events have no memory. The past doesn't make anything due.
